# Where the Light Is 🎸

John Mayer has long been my favorite music artist!! from his tasteful guitar solos to his beautiful songwriting and vocal depth. I’ve been to a few of his concerts, and he always manages to choose a setlist that is unique while still makes sure we get all the hits. I wondered how those setlists stacked up against each other. That led to my motivating question:

### **What can I learn about how John Mayer builds his concert setlists?**

Below, I walk through how I acquired the data and highlight the most interesting findings from my exploratory data analysis.

![John Mayer](JohnMayerin2019.png){width=50% fig-align="center"}

---

# Data Acquisition 

To build the dataset I wanted, I pulled from multiple online sources.

### **Primary API used**
- **Setlist.fm API** — provided detailed information about each concert, including:
  - venue  
  - city  
  - tour  
  - date  
  - complete setlist  
  - encore structure  

### **Secondary API (attempted)**
I originally planned to also integrate:
- **Spotify Web API** — for audio features like tempo, energy, valence, etc.

Although I was able to access the api for Spotify, integrating the features cleanly took more time and effort than expected, so I proceeded with Setlist.fm alone for this version. My GitHub repo still includes the partial Spotify integration work. In a future project, I want to return to this analysis and add in those spotify features. 

### **GitHub Repo (Code + Data)**
👉 [John Mayer Setlist Project Repo](https://github.com/chamiltonb8/stat_386_music-John-Mayer)

# Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

After cleaning and merging, my dataset contained:
- most common songs  
- rare songs  
- concert cities  
- set lengths  
- song order behavior  
- growth of his live catalog over time  

Below are some of the clearest insights.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("final_setlists_john_mayer.csv", parse_dates=["show_date"])
df.head()
```

## Most Common Songs

Here are the most-played songs across all concerts in the dataset. What surprised me most is that “Who Says” appears much more often than I expected. (about 14 times)“Slow Dancing in a Burning Room” His most recognizalbe song is number one right where I would expect it to be. 

```{python}
song_counts = (
    df.groupby("song")["show_id"]
      .nunique()
      .sort_values(ascending=False)
      .head(15)
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

# reverse for nicer top-to-bottom ordering
songs = song_counts.index.tolist()[::-1]
counts = song_counts.values.tolist()[::-1]

plt.barh(songs, counts)
plt.xlabel("Number of Shows Played")
plt.ylabel("Song")
plt.title("Top 15 Most-Played Songs Across Shows")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


## Cities He's visited the Most

John Mayer has visited Los Angeles the Most for his shows (He does have a house there)! this is a cool chart that also shows that Amsterdam was the second most visited. 

```{python}
city_counts = (
    df.groupby("city")["show_id"]
      .nunique()
      .sort_values(ascending=False)
      .head(10)
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
cities = city_counts.index.tolist()[::-1]
counts = city_counts.values.tolist()[::-1]

plt.barh(cities, counts)
plt.xlabel("Number of Shows")
plt.ylabel("City")
plt.title("Top 10 Cities for John Mayer Shows")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Distribution of Song Positions in Setlists

I found it cool that there were a few concerts that only had one song! 

```{python}
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.hist(df["position"], bins=range(1, df["position"].max() + 2), edgecolor="black")
plt.xlabel("Song Position in Set")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.title("Distribution of Song Positions in Setlists")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


## Rarest Songs

Here are the 20 rarest songs to hear at a John Mayer Concert! 

```{python}
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("final_setlists_john_mayer.csv")

rarity = (
    df.dropna(subset=["rarity"])
      .groupby("song")["rarity"]
      .first()
      .sort_values()
)

print("🎸 Rarest John Mayer Songs in These Setlists:\n")
for song, r in rarity.head(20).items():  # top 20 rarest
    print(f"{song} — rarity: {r:.3f}")
```

## Growth of Unique Songs Per Concert over time

How quickly does John's live catalog grow? This line chart shows when each song first appeared and how his total number of unique songs increased over time.

```{python}
# Drop missing dates
df2 = df.dropna(subset=["show_date"]).copy()

# Sort chronologically
df2 = df2.sort_values("show_date")

# Identify when each song FIRST appeared
first_plays = df2.groupby("song")["show_date"].min().sort_values()

# Create cumulative count over time
first_plays_df = (
    first_plays
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"show_date": "first_play_date"})
    .sort_values("first_play_date")
)

first_plays_df["cumulative_unique_songs"] = range(1, len(first_plays_df) + 1)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(first_plays_df["first_play_date"],
         first_plays_df["cumulative_unique_songs"],
         marker="o", markersize=3, linewidth=1)

plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Unique Songs")
plt.title("Growth of John Mayer’s Live Song Catalog Over Time")
plt.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Song Popularity Over Time

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("final_setlists_john_mayer.csv", parse_dates=["show_date"])

song_name = "In Your Atmosphere"   # you can change this to any song

df_song = df[df["song"] == song_name].dropna(subset=["show_date"])
df_song = df_song.sort_values("show_date")

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(df_song["show_date"], range(1, len(df_song)+1), marker="o")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Plays")
plt.title(f"Cumulative Live Performances of '{song_name}' Over Time")
plt.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# One More Thing: The top 10 openers and closers! 
```{python}
openers = (
    df[df["is_opener"] == 1]
    .groupby("song")["show_id"]
    .nunique()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
)

closers = (
    df[df["is_closer"] == 1]
    .groupby("song")["show_id"]
    .nunique()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.barh(openers.index[::-1], openers.values[::-1], color="navy")
plt.xlabel("Number of Times Used as Opener")
plt.title("Top 10 Openers")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.barh(closers.index[::-1], closers.values[::-1], color="maroon")
plt.xlabel("Number of Times Used as Closer")
plt.title("Top 10 Closers")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
